newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: FEATURE - Colombia looks to private firms to upgrade railways.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Colombia looks to private firms to upgrade railways.

text.p: Colombia will be looking to get its decrepit railway network back on the right track by auctioning off concessions to private enterprise in mid to late November.

The challenge facing prospective operators is to get the 40 percent of the network currently in total disrepair back into service and upgrade other sections to allow rail to compete with road in moving the nation's cargo -- chiefly coffee, coal, bananas, iron and steel.

The rewards for the eventual winners of the 30-year concessions include a predicted rail cargo bonanza, with demand forecast to increase more than tenfold by 2002, according to the U.S.-Spanish independent consultancy Socimer-Ineco, which has drawn up guidelines for the bidding process.
If all goes well in cargo operations the concessionaires could also get the chance to offer passenger services -- virtually non-existent at present.

"Rail transport is almost dead at the moment and what we want to do is to help give back a service to the country and take some of the cargo off the roads since they too are affected by poor maintenance," Jorge Enrique Hincapie, deputy chairman of the state rail company Ferrovias, told Reuters.

At present, just 0.9 percent of Colombia's estimated 90 million tonnes of cargo a year is moved on railways -- which were built by independent companies with the help of foreign engineers, particularly Francisco Javier Cisneros of Cuba, in the latter half of the 19th and early 20th centuries.
If Socimer-Ineco's estimates, based on a return to the percentage of cargo by rail in 1970 figures, prove correct, in excess of 14.5 million tonnes annually could be carried by rail within six years.
The 940-mile (1,500 km) Atlantic network will be the first to come under the gavel while the 405-mile (650 km) Pacific network is scheduled to be opened to bidding next April.
The successful bidders will not pay a cent to the Colombian government but will make a commitment to invest a certain amount in track upgrades, maintenance and rolling stock.

For its part, the state will not wash its hands of the rail network -- little more than a sickly white elephant at present -- but has agreed to pump in about $580 million as its contribution to righting years of neglect, Hincapie said.

Bidding was originally due to open on October 7 but was delayed until Ferrovias prepared detailed estimates of its future budgetary commitments to the rail network -- a process still not completed, according to Hincapie.

More than $220 million of repair projects are already under way along the Atlantic line. An extra $205 million in joint state-private investment is needed to make routes fully serviceable, according to the Socimer-Ineco study. On the Pacific line, Hincapie said Ferrovias was likely to foot the entire $189 million needed for essential repair and maintenance work.
Hincapie said he expected the winning bid would be a pledge in future maintenance, upgrades and new stock worth between $60 million and $100 million on each of the two networks.

"It was calculated we would have to contribute heavily to infrastructure projects to allow the concessionaires to make some profits, otherwise nobody would be interested. The deterioration of the tracks has been due to lack of investment in maintenance over the years," he explained.

Hincapie said U.S. rail companies Anacostia and Pacific, Railroad Development Corporation, Wisconsin Central Transportation Company, Noel Group and Western Rail, Chile's Cruz Blanca, Renfe of Spain, France's SNCF and German enterprise Ferrostal had expressed interest.
Bidding restrictions rule out direct bids from the existing two Colombian rail companies, but they would be permitted to form consortia with foreign concerns.
If all goes to plan, the two new rail concessions could be transporting goods more quickly and more cheaply than trucking companies by the year 2002, Hincapie believes.

With little unionised labour, rail offers a valuable alternative to exporters and industrialists, he said. He added that trains were less vulnerable than trucks to common crime and piracy, but conceded that Colombia's three main guerrilla groups could easily target railways for attack if they became a key player in the national economy.

Under a system introduced in 1989, track maintenance and rail traffic supervision comes under the control of Ferrovias. Transport operations are carried out by two joint state-private ventures, the Colombian Rail Transport Company in the Atlantic zone, and the Western Rail Transport Country in Pacific coastal area. Both operating contracts expire in 1997.
